source: Newell, Shaw and Simon (1959) Report on a general problem-solving program (IFIP Congress, pp 256-264)
finding: Founding report of GPS. A problem is a start state and a goal state. GPS finds the difference between them, picks an operator tied to that kind of difference, and if the operator cannot be applied yet it sets the missing precondition as a new subgoal. Knowledge of the task is kept apart from the general solver.
numbers: Citation (venue, pages) confirmed from the Wikipedia GPS page. RAND PDF returned HTTP 403, so no numbers.
limits: Not opened this session; recalled from standard accounts. Verify before relying on it.
agent_relevance: This is the loop O5 needs: measure the gap, choose a move that targets the gap, turn a blocked move into a subgoal.

source: Newell and Simon (1961) GPS, a program that simulates human thought
finding: First comparison of GPS traces with thinking-aloud protocols of people solving logic problems. The claim was that program and person use similar goal types (transform, reduce difference, apply operator) and similar subgoal structure.
numbers: No numbers recorded (paywalled).
limits: Not opened this session; recalled from standard accounts. Verify before relying on it. The match was judged by the authors on few protocols, not by blind raters.
agent_relevance: Supports difference reduction as a model of human subgoal choice, as a weak prior only.

source: Ernst and Newell (1969) GPS: A case study in generality and problem solving (Academic Press)
finding: Rewrote GPS so task knowledge (objects, operators, difference table) is data and the solver is fixed. Ran it on about ten task environments, for example symbolic integration, Missionaries and Cannibals, Tower of Hanoi and parsing.
numbers: Number of task domains recalled as about 10 to 11; not verified.
limits: Not opened this session; recalled from standard accounts. Verify before relying on it. The hand-built difference tables did much of the work, so generality was partial.
agent_relevance: In our agent the difference table is the weak point: the model must name the gap and the operator for it in task words.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026-11-01) General Problem Solver
finding: GPS was written in IPL by Newell, Shaw and Simon at RAND. It was the first program to separate problem knowledge from a generic solver. It solved toy problems such as Tower of Hanoi but not real-world problems, because the search blew up. Its line led to Soar.
numbers: Related reports cited: Newell (1963) GPS-2-2 guide, RAND RM-3337-PR; Ernst and Newell (1969); Newell and Simon (1972) Human Problem Solving.
limits: Secondary source. Dates inside the page disagree (1957 vs 1959).
agent_relevance: Pure difference reduction does not scale; it needs pruning and a progress check.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026-11-01) Means-ends analysis
finding: MEA: given current state and goal, choose an action that reduces the difference, apply it, recurse. The system must link each detectable difference to actions that reduce it, and must detect its own progress because some action sequences fail. If differences have known importance, handle the most important first. GPS used a hand-written table of connections; STRIPS and PRODIGY made the link task independent.
numbers: No experiments with numbers on the page.
limits: Secondary and tagged as needing citations. It lists Sweller (1988) as the reason MEA is not always advised for human learners.
agent_relevance: Two design needs for O5: a difference-to-operator link and a progress detector.

source: Fikes and Nilsson (1971) STRIPS: a new approach to the application of theorem proving to problem solving
finding: STRIPS kept the means-ends idea but computed differences from the goal formula and chose operators by their add lists, so no hand table was needed. Operators have preconditions, add lists and delete lists.
numbers: No numbers; paper not opened (ScienceDirect 403, Stanford host unreachable).
limits: Not opened this session; recalled from standard accounts. Verify before relying on it. Linear subgoal ordering is the known flaw.
agent_relevance: Right data shape for O5 operators: precondition, effect, and what it destroys.

source: Sussman anomaly and non-linear planning (Sussman 1975; Chapman 1987 Planning for conjunctive goals)
finding: Classic boundary condition for means-ends planning. In a three-block world, solving goals one after the other (linear MEA) fails or gives a bad plan, because finishing one goal undoes another. Non-linear planners keep subgoal order open.
numbers: Standard three-block example; no experimental numbers.
limits: Not opened this session; recalled from standard accounts. Verify before relying on it.
agent_relevance: Guardrail idea: after each subgoal, re-check the earlier subgoals. An LLM run shows the same slip (see a24).

source: Laird, Newell and Rosenbloom (1987) Soar: an architecture for general intelligence
finding: Soar treats means-ends analysis as a weak method that appears when the system hits an impasse and makes a subgoal for it. Chunking turns solved subgoals into rules so search is not repeated.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened this session; recalled from standard accounts. Verify before relying on it.
agent_relevance: Matches G1: open a subgoal on an impasse signal, not on a schedule. Chunking suggests storing solved subgoals for reuse.

source: Larkin, McDermott, Simon and Simon (1980) Expert and novice performance in solving physics problems, Science 208
finding: Novices in physics tend to work backward from the unknown with means-ends steps. Experts work forward from the givens using known principles, and mostly do not search.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened this session; recalled from standard accounts. Verify before relying on it. Observational comparison, not a training experiment.
agent_relevance: MEA is the fallback of a solver without schemas. A strong model with a matching schema may do better going forward than hunting for gaps.

source: Sweller, Mawer and Ward (1983) Development of expertise in mathematical problem solving, JEP: General 112
finding: Practice on problems that invite means-ends search led to less rule learning than practice that did not. Means-ends search uses working memory on the gap and operator choice, leaving little for learning structure.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened this session; recalled from standard accounts. Verify before relying on it.
agent_relevance: Search spends budget that could go to learning. For a one-shot agent, gap-driven search costs context.

source: Sweller (1988) Cognitive load during problem solving: effects on learning, Cognitive Science 12
finding: Argues means-ends analysis loads working memory because the solver holds current state, goal, difference and candidate operators at once, which blocks schema learning. Worked examples and goal-free problems avoid that load.
numbers: Citation confirmed through Wikipedia; Wiley PDF returned HTTP 403. No numbers.
limits: Not opened this session; recalled from standard accounts. Verify before relying on it. Cognitive load is a theory; effects were measured on learning, not on solving.
agent_relevance: MEA is costly bookkeeping. Code should hold state, goal and gap so the model does not.

source: Owen and Sweller (1985) What do students learn while solving mathematics problems? J Educ Psychol 77
finding: Goal-free geometry problems ('find as many angles as you can') produced faster learning than specific-goal problems that induce means-ends search.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened this session; recalled from standard accounts. Verify before relying on it.
agent_relevance: A goal-free probe (forward exploration) may beat gap-chasing when the agent has no model of the domain.

source: Vollmeyer, Burns and Holyoak (1996) The impact of goal specificity on strategy use and the acquisition of problem structure, Cognitive Science 20
finding: Learners with a nonspecific goal tested hypotheses more systematically and learned system structure better than learners with a specific goal, who used difference reduction.
numbers: No numbers recorded (Wiley 403).
limits: Not opened this session; recalled from standard accounts. Verify before relying on it. The effect is on structure knowledge; solving the one target problem can be as good with a specific goal.
agent_relevance: Boundary for O5: use gap-driven choice when the domain model is known; explore first when it is not.

source: Atwood and Polson (1976) A process model for water jug problems, Cognitive Psychology 8
finding: Process model of the water jug task: choose the move that gets closest to the goal with very limited look-ahead, plus memory for recent states. It fit people's move choice better than full search.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened this session; recalled from standard accounts. Verify before relying on it.
agent_relevance: People seem to use shallow one-step gap checks, which fits a cheap code-checked gap score.

source: Jeffries, Polson, Razran and Atwood (1977) A process model for Missionaries-Cannibals and other river-crossing problems, Cognitive Psychology 9
finding: People avoid moves that look like going away from the goal. Steps that must temporarily raise the difference, such as taking people back across the river, are the hard points.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened this session; recalled from standard accounts. Verify before relying on it. Wording of the finding is from memory.
agent_relevance: Key limit of gap reduction: some solutions need a step that increases the gap. O5 needs a rule for allowed detours.

source: Simon (1975) The functional equivalence of problem solving skills, Cognitive Psychology 7
finding: Tower of Hanoi can be solved by several strategies (goal-recursive, perceptual, move-pattern) that give the same output. People often shift from means-ends to perceptual strategies with practice.
numbers: No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened this session; recalled from standard accounts. Verify before relying on it.
agent_relevance: Different procedures give the same answer, so the agent should log which strategy ran, not only the answer.

source: Kotovsky, Hayes and Simon (1985) Why are some problems hard? Cognitive Psychology 17
finding: Isomorphs of the Tower of Hanoi differ greatly in difficulty, roughly a factor of 16 in solution time. The harder version loads working memory with more rules, so the same state space is not the same problem.
numbers: The factor of 16 is recalled from memory and not verified.
limits: Not opened this session; recalled from standard accounts. Verify before relying on it.
agent_relevance: Same logic, different wording, big change in success. Test O5 on paraphrased and obfuscated forms.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking: understanding strengths and limitations of reasoning models via the lens of problem complexity
finding: Reasoning models were tested on Tower of Hanoi, Checker Jumping, River Crossing and Blocks World with controlled size N. Three regimes: standard models do as well or better at low N, thinking models win at medium N, both collapse to near zero at high N. Thinking effort rises with N, then falls near the collapse point.
numbers: Claude 3.7 Sonnet thinking was near-perfect on Hanoi N=5 (31 moves) but failed River Crossing at N=3 (11 moves). First Hanoi error often near move 100 at N=10. Hanoi accuracy near zero from N>=8 (255 moves). Trace analysis used 25 samples per model and size.
limits: Output budget and format are disputed (see a20). Familiarity with the puzzle likely explains the gap between puzzles.
agent_relevance: Hanoi is the standard means-ends test. Models do not reliably run long goal-subgoal procedures; keep subgoal depth short or run the stack in code.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) Illusion of Thinking, algorithm-given experiment (Sec 4.4 and appendix)
finding: Giving the models the full recursive Hanoi algorithm in the prompt did not move the collapse point. Executing a given algorithm failed at about the same size as devising a plan.
numbers: Collapse stayed at roughly the same N for Tower of Hanoi and Checker Jumping with the algorithm given. DeepSeek-R1 at temperature 0 collapsed at N=8.
quote: even when we provide the algorithm in the prompt--so that the model only needs to execute the prescribed steps--performance does not improve
limits: Authors read this as an execution and verification limit. Critics say token limits explain it.
agent_relevance: Knowing the subgoal procedure is not enough. The program should carry the subgoal stack, not the model.

source: Lawsen (2025) The Illusion of the Illusion of Thinking (comment on Shojaee et al.)
finding: Argues the collapse is mostly an evaluation artefact. Models write 'to avoid making this too long, I'll stop here'. Some River Crossing cases (N>=6, boat capacity 3) are impossible but were scored as failures. Asking for a function that prints the Hanoi solution restored high accuracy.
numbers: Hanoi N=15 as a Lua function: very high accuracy for Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Claude Opus 4, o3 and Gemini 2.5, under 5,000 tokens. Estimated output limit: about 12-13 disks at 64,000 tokens, with 10 tokens per move.
limits: Preliminary, no full table. An earlier draft had a wrong token model and was revised. Written with an LLM co-author.
agent_relevance: Separate 'cannot plan' from 'cannot write out a long plan'. For O5, ask for the subgoal rule or code, not the whole move list.

source: Meyerson et al. (2025) Solving a million-step LLM task with zero errors (MAKER)
finding: Hanoi with 20 disks (over one million dependent steps) was solved with zero errors by extreme decomposition into single-step microagents, with voting and red-flagging. The authors say a 1% per-step error rate means failure after about 100 steps of a million-step task.
numbers: 20 disks = 2^20 - 1 = 1,048,575 steps. A 1-in-1,000 per-step error rate sounds low but fails at this scale.
limits: Each microagent is given the overall strategy and the current state, so this tests execution, not discovery of subgoals.
agent_relevance: Supports code-held state and one-step model calls. Voting works only if errors are not correlated (G4).

source: Valmeekam, Marquez, Olmo, Sreedharan and Kambhampati (2023) PlanBench
finding: Benchmark of planning in Blocksworld and Logistics: plan generation, optimal planning, replanning, plan reuse and more. GPT-4 and Instruct-GPT3 do poorly on Blocksworld; scores fall on obfuscated versions, which points to pattern matching.
numbers: Plain Blocksworld plan generation: GPT-4 34.3%, Instruct-GPT3 6.8%. Mystery Blocksworld deceptive: GPT-4 26/600 (4.3%), Instruct-GPT3 0.23%. Randomised: GPT-4 12/600 (2%), Instruct-GPT3 6/600 (1%).
limits: 2023 models at temperature 0. Later reasoning models score far higher on plain Blocksworld.
agent_relevance: Blocksworld is the home ground of MEA. An obfuscation test shows whether the agent plans or recalls.

source: Valmeekam, Sreedharan, Marquez, Olmo and Kambhampati (2023) On the planning abilities of large language models
finding: Autonomous plan generation by LLMs is poor (about 3% of plans executable on average). As a heuristic source for an AI planner or as advice to human planners it helps a little.
numbers: Human baseline: 39 of 50 (78%) valid plans, 35 of 39 (89.7%) optimal. Plan generation: GPT-3 6/600 (1%), Instruct-GPT3 41/600 (6.8%), BLOOM 4/250 (1.6%). Human-in-the-loop: 17/23 (74%) vs 18/22 (82%) correct final plans with and without LLM suggestion.
limits: Small human samples; 2022 models. Authors argue LLMs are better as heuristic guides than as planners.
agent_relevance: LLM as move proposer under a checker beats LLM as full planner. This matches the schema's split of labour.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with language model is planning with world model (RAP)
finding: Search over actions with the LLM as a world model that predicts the next state. On Blocksworld, LLaMA-33B with RAP beat chain of thought by a wide margin. The case study shows CoT going for the second goal first and breaking the first goal; RAP recovers by exploring other paths.
numbers: Success for plans of 2/4/6 steps: CoT 0.17/0.02/0.00; CoT pass@10 0.23/0.07/0.00; CoT with GPT-4 0.50/0.63/0.40; RAP(10) 1.00/0.86/0.26; RAP(20) 1.00/0.88/0.42. Authors report an average success of 64%.
limits: Many LLM calls per problem; one benchmark family; the GPT-4 baseline is plain CoT.
agent_relevance: A live LLM example of the Sussman anomaly: greedy subgoal order breaks earlier goals. Re-check earlier subgoals after each step.

source: Kazemi et al. (2023) LAMBADA: backward chaining for automated reasoning in natural language
finding: Reasoning from the goal back to the facts (a goal-directed cousin of MEA) beat forward-chaining methods on deep proofs. Forward selection-inference gets worse as the theory grows and repeats facts.
numbers: ProofWriter depth-5 (50 sampled correct-label examples): CoT produced correct proof chains for only 28%; hallucination was the main error (48%). Selection-Inference, failed cases: only 29% had no redundant facts; 7% repeated the same inference 5 times. Reported relative gains at depth 5: 44% over CoT and 56% over SI (ProofWriter-PUD).
limits: Synthetic rule data. Backward chaining here is proof search, not difference reduction.
agent_relevance: Goal-first decomposition helps where forward search explodes. Supports offering a backward option at O5 for deep tasks.

source: Gandhi et al. (2025) Cognitive behaviors that enable self-improving reasoners, or, four habits of highly effective STaRs
finding: Four behaviours (verification, backtracking, subgoal setting, backward chaining) separate base models that improve under RL on Countdown from those that do not. Priming a weak model with these behaviours, even with wrong solutions, closes the gap.
numbers: After RL, Qwen-2.5-3B reached about 60% on Countdown vs about 30% for Llama-3.2-3B. Empty or placeholder thoughts stayed at 30-35%. Priming with incorrect solutions that had the right behaviours matched correct-solution priming. On GPQA, curated pretraining raised subgoal setting to 6.5 instances per question vs 0.7 in the control, with no score gain (both about 12%).
limits: 3B models, one game, RL training. In the all-strategies run, RL kept backtracking and verification and suppressed subgoal setting and backward chaining.
agent_relevance: Subgoal talk transfers but did not by itself raise accuracy. Do not credit subgoals without a check.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: deliberate problem solving with large language models
finding: Search over partial thoughts with LLM evaluation of each state. It cites Newell, Shaw and Simon (1959) and Newell and Simon (1972) as the source of problem solving as search. On Game of 24 it beat chain of thought.
numbers: Game of 24 success: IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC (k=100) 9.0%, ToT b=1 45%, ToT b=5 74%, IO best of 100 33%, CoT best of 100 49%.
limits: GPT-4, one main task. The LLM both proposes and judges states, which G5 warns against.
agent_relevance: Gap-style state rating (sure/maybe/impossible) worked, but the model did the judging. Move the check into code where possible.

source: Prasad et al. (2023) ADaPT: as-needed decomposition and planning with language models
finding: Decompose a subtask only when the executor fails (an impasse), recursively. This is Soar-style subgoaling on impasse. It beat ReAct, plan-and-execute and retry baselines.
numbers: ALFWorld overall success: ADaPT 71.6 vs ReAct 43.3 and Plan-and-Execute 43.3. WebShop success: ADaPT 44.0 vs ReAct 32.0 and Plan-and-Execute 17.0. TextCraft: ADaPT 52.0 vs ReAct 19.0 and Plan-and-Execute 27.0. Abstract: gains up to 28.3, 27 and 33 points.
limits: Single-run numbers; a GPT-3.5-class executor in the main table; planner and executor from the same family.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G1: decompose on a failure signal, not up front.

source: Katz, Kokel, Srinivas and Sohrabi (2024, v3 2026) Thought of Search: planning with language models through the lens of efficiency
finding: Many LLM planning methods (ToT, RAP, GoT, LATS) give up soundness and completeness and use huge numbers of model calls. Having the LLM write the successor and goal-test code, then running ordinary search, solved whole datasets at 100% with a few calls.
numbers: Claim: 100% accuracy on four search tasks (24 Game, Crossword, BlocksWorld, PrOntoQA); BlocksWorld instances have 4 to 5 blocks.
limits: Needs a formal state model that code can run; open-ended text states are harder.
agent_relevance: Let code do state transitions and the gap count; the model writes only the move generator or the check.

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024) LLMs can't plan, but can help planning in LLM-Modulo frameworks
finding: Position paper. LLMs generate candidate plans; external verifiers check them in a loop. States that on average only about 12% of LLM-generated plans were executable in the authors' tests.
numbers: About 12% executable plans (as stated in the paper text).
limits: Position paper; the figure is the authors' own summary.
agent_relevance: Same split as the schema: model proposes, code verifies.

source: Frontiers in Psychology (2024) Biological evolution and human cognition are analogous information processing systems
finding: Describes means-ends as: consider current state, goal state, differences, then a move that reduces them; common in closed problems with few moves. Says this costs working memory and that worked examples remove those steps.
numbers: No new data.
limits: Theory summary by cognitive-load authors; not independent evidence.
agent_relevance: MEA needs four things held at once (state, goal, gap, operator).

source: Behavioral Sciences (2025) Human cognitive architecture as an intelligent natural information processing system
finding: Argues means-ends analysis is a general method for new domains that may itself need explicit teaching, and that many problem-solving courses are built on Newell and Simon (1972) variants. This disputes the cognitive-load view that general strategies need no teaching.
numbers: No new data.
limits: Position article.
agent_relevance: Open dispute on whether general strategies must be taught. For a model, put the strategy in the scaffold rather than hope it appears.

source: Korean J Med Educ (2019) Reasoning processes in clinical reasoning: from the perspective of cognitive psychology
finding: Summarises Anderson's three ways to solve complex problems: means-ends analysis, working backward, planning by simplification. MEA fits when options are few or many subgoals lead to the goal; working backward spends time removing wrong answers to find root causes.
numbers: No data.
limits: Textbook-style review; secondary.
agent_relevance: A rule of thumb for choosing gap-forward or backward mode at O5.

source: Psychometrika (2026) Two Markov solution process models for the assessment of planning in problem solving
finding: Notes that Tower of London tasks require planning in terms of means-ends analysis and that what they measure is still unresolved. Builds Markov models of solution processes.
numbers: Details not extracted (only the opening paragraphs were read).
limits: Only the introduction was read. Psychometric model, not an MEA test.
agent_relevance: Tower tasks can be scored by process, not only final success; useful for scoring agent traces.
